Submission received: 19 December 2021 / Revised: 29 January 2022 / Accepted: 7 February 2022 / Published: 11 February 2022 Abstract In this study, we use the critical slowing down (CSD) theory to identify the precursory anomalies of groundwater radon based on the 1000-day continuous data from 8 monitoring stations in Yunnan Province, China during the seismically active period of 1993–1996. The low-frequency and high-frequency information were extracted from raw groundwater radon data to calculate their one-step lag autocorrelation (AR-1) and variance, respectively, in order to identify the precursory anomalies. The results show that the anomaly characteristics can be divided into three categories: sudden jump anomalies, persistent anomalies, and fluctuation anomalies. The highest average seismic recognition rate is 72.78%, based on the high-frequency information’s autocorrelation, while the lowest is 45.08%, based on the low-frequency information’s variance. The crustal activity and the change in hydrogeological conditions are possibly the main factors influencing groundwater radon anomalies in the selected period in the study area. There is a positive correlation between the anomaly occurrence time and epicentral distance when epicentral distance is less than 300 km, which may be related to the seismogenic modes and hydrogeological conditions. This study provides a reference for identifying groundwater radon anomalies before earthquakes by mathematical methods. 1. Introduction Earthquake disasters are important global issues concerning the development of human society, which can often be highly destructive due to the lack of early warning systems [1]. The geochemistry anomalies related to earthquakes are important research directions in the search for earthquake precursors with potential use in earthquake prediction [2]. With the improvement in the monitoring system, radon, which is considered as one of the key indicators of the geochemistry, has increasingly attracted the attention of researchers [3,4,5]. Radon is generated by the decay of 238U in rock and soil in the subsurface environment, and therefore remains in the soil or dissolves in groundwater. There are many published studies on the relationship between radon and earthquakes, suggesting that radon has the potential to be a good indicator of the precursory process [6]. It was first proposed in 1927 that radon anomalies in groundwater were related to earthquakes, but it was not until 30 years later that people collected accurate data showing the change in radon concentrations in groundwater before earthquakes [7,8]. The temperature, precipitation, and other meteorological factors can cause the seasonal variation in groundwater radon concentrations, but its anomalies may also be related to the change in tectonic stress [7,9]. Although it has become a consensus that radon anomalies could be related to earthquakes, it is generally very difficult to identify anomalies because radon concentration variations often show the characteristics of nonlinear dynamic fluctuations. Therefore, it is very necessary to find effective identification methods. The traditional statistical methods, to a certain degree, are subjective and inaccurate. Some data mining methods, such as machine learning and artificial neural networks, have been used recently and have made a few achievements [7,9,10,11]. Faced with the complexity of crustal movements, many scholars began to perform systematic statistical analysis [12,13]. In 1989, Bak [14] proposed the “self-organized criticality (SOC) phenomenon” and classified earthquakes as this phenomenon, which attracted seismic researchers’ attention to the precursor analysis of the critical threshold of complex dynamic systems [15,16]. With the in-depth study of complex systems in medicine, finance, ecology and other fields [17,18,19], scholars have found that many complex systems have critical points, before and after which the state of the system will change; the critical point is also called an “avalanche” in SOC phenomena [20]. Accordingly, how to identify the critical point has become the key issue in complex systems research. The critical slowing down (CSD) theory has been widely used to indicate the critical point of complex systems, such as the critical state’s identification in clinical medicine, biological systems and climate change, etc. [21,22,23]. The CSD is a phenomenon before the tipping point, which is where a complex system shifts abruptly from a state to another state [24]. For earthquakes, the high stress state before a large earthquake is considered as before the critical point, and the stress release after the earthquake is after the critical point, so the earthquake can be regarded as the critical point. Before the earthquake, the fluctuation amplitude of the corresponding observation value increases and the recovery speed slows down until the occurrence of the earthquake. Numerous studies have found indicators that can reflect the CSD effectively [25]. fetched_contents.text: Main features of hydrogeodynamic earthquake precursors Research paper Main features of hydrogeodynamic earthquake precursors Abstract An analysis of available data on hydrogeodynamic precursors of large earthquakes in different regions of the world is presented. These precursors were registered by variations of groundwater level before 31 earthquakes with magnitudes between 4.5 and 8.0. We investigated some features of the precursors, such as the signal amplitude, shape and time, as well as some precursor indices, as functions of magnitude and epicentral distance. In most cases, groundwater level variations before earthquakes have extreme values. A new index, the precursor extremum time, has been defined for such precursors. It has been found that this index, as well as the amplitude of groundwater level variations, correlates well with precursor time. The hydrogeodynamic precursor time and signal amplitude do not show sufficiently close correlative relationships with earthquake magnitude and epicentral distance. At the same time, there is a trend of increasing precursor time and amplitude with the growth of earthquake magnitude, and an inversed relationship for epicentral distance. These properties of hydrogeodynamic precursors seem to be associated with geodynamic processes developing in an extensive area during the preparation of a large earthquake. Manifestations of these precursors also depend on the tensosensitivity of the borehole-aquifer system which controls the transformation of strain into the hydrogeodynamic precursory response. fetched_contents.text: New observations in Central Italy of groundwater responses to the worldwide seismicity Introduction Earthquakes are among the main natural processes that can cause the strongest perturbations in the Earth’s crust. Seismic events can change crustal stress, both static and dynamic, in the co-seismic and post-seismic phases. Static stress is generated by fault loading and its release mostly occurs in the near-field whereas dynamic stress is triggered by fault slip, generating the migration of seismic waves and, for this reason, its perturbation also spreads to the far-field. Many studies have highlighted the sensitivity of fluid behaviour related to the modification of the stress field, both the static and the dynamic one1,2. In particular, hydrogeological and geochemical responses include: changes in groundwater level3,4,5, temperature6,7, water chemistry8,9,10, stream flow11,12,13, and gas geochemistry14,15,16,17,18. Among these parameters, a change in groundwater level is more commonly recorded due to the simplicity of doing so through the use of inexpensive devices. In fractured high-permeability aquifers, like the one studied in this work, impulsive changes in the water table are frequent, also due to classical hydrogeological causes. Various mechanisms have been proposed to explain groundwater level responses to earthquakes including: (1) poroelastic response to co-seismic static strain19; (2) undrained consolidation of sediments20; (3) clogging–unclogging of pores and fractures by oscillatory flows produced by the passage of seismic waves3,21,22; (4) co-seismic gas bubble development23,24; (5) shaking-induced compaction or dilatation25. Depending on the mechanism involved, the temporal pattern of groundwater level variation can vary significantly and, hence, can be symptomatic of specific mechanisms. Previous studies have highlighted permanent and transient signals that are characterized by step-like and/or spike-like temporal changes both upward and/or downward26,27,28. Only a few studies have reported groundwater level variations induced by earthquakes that are very far away from the observation point, known as ‘teleseism’3,25,26,29,30. According to the USGS a teleseism is a tremor related to seismic events occurring more than 1000 km away31. To investigate the relationship between groundwater characteristics and the seismic cycle, two multiparameter probes were installed in a 50 m and a 100 m deep groundwater wells (PF60.2 and PF60.3) in the Central Apennines (Italy, Fig. 1, see “Material and methods” section) in 2014. These wells were part of a monitoring test site in fractured carbonate aquifers, developed for the identification of potential hydrogeochemical precursors of earthquakes5,9. After their installation (July 2014 for PF60.3 and November 2014 for PF60.2) the probe in the PF60.3 well recorded significant changes in groundwater level following the occurrence of many high magnitude earthquakes around the world (Mw ≥ 6.5). In this paper, we present the results of the water level monitoring with a view to expanding the understanding of perturbations of fluids in the upper crust due to earthquakes, with a focus on groundwater–earthquake physical relationships. Since these or similar probes are used by us and other geoscientists to identify potential hydrogeochemical precursors to nearby earthquakes2,5,9,20,33,34, identifying and thus filtering the effect on (and also the cause of) the groundwater level induced by distant earthquakes is a pre-requisite to understanding the possible effect induced by the seismic cycle of nearby faults. Geological and hydrogeological settings The Central Apennines fold-and-thrust belt was formed by tectonic accretion and the following backarc extension during the Oligocene-Quaternary ‘westward’ subduction and ‘eastward’ retreat of the Adriatic plate beneath the European plate. This segment of mountain chain is characterized by NE-verging thrusts, which dissect the tectonic edifice into several thick tectonic sheets35. The post-accretion extensional regime, which has dominated the Central Apennines from the Pliocene onwards, has segmented the orogenic edifice and determined the current structural setting. The development, in particular, of NW-striking extensional faults has been responsible of intra-mountain basin formation (e.g. the Campo Imperatore, L’Aquila, Fucino, and Sulmona basins). These basins are mostly half-grabens filled by Upper Pliocene and Pleistocene continental deposits. Precursory groundwater anomalies have been detected at a range that is mostly near the epicenter, but some studies also report anomalies at more distant locations. The evidence suggests that the largest-amplitude anomalies tend to occur closest to the epicenter, with the greatest anomalies reported closest to the epicenters and perhaps for the largest earthquakes [N1-R3]. In hydrogeodynamic studies, the precursory anomalies tend to occur close to the eventual epicenter of the earthquake [N1-R2], and the physical models indicate that this proximity is likely tied to the hydrogeological and geodynamic conditions [N1-R2][N1-F1]. The same review also states that the hydrogeodynamic precursor time and signal amplitude do not show sufficiently close correlative relationships with earthquake magnitude and epicentral distance, but there is a trend of increasing precursor time and amplitude with growing earthquake magnitude and an inverse relationship with epicentral distance [N1-F2].

The types of groundwater signals observed are not limited to one class. The most direct evidence comes from groundwater radon anomalies, which are identified using critical slowing down theory in a Yunnan case study [N1-F1]. The review also explicitly mentions hydrogeodynamic precursors registered by variations of groundwater level before 31 earthquakes with magnitudes between 4.5 and 8.0 [N1-F2]. Another study explicitly links groundwater responses to earthquakes to changes in groundwater level, temperature, water chemistry, and gas geochemistry [N2-F3]. In the Turkish spring-water study, anomalies included electrical conductivity and ion concentration changes in spring waters before moderate-magnitude earthquakes [N3-F4]. So the signals are broad and include both level and chemistry-based anomalies, with radon and conductivity as particularly prominent examples [N1-F1][N2-F3][N3-F4].

Anomalies are usually localized rather than regional. The hydrogeodynamic precursor literature emphasizes that groundwater level variations before earthquakes have extreme values and that the signal depends on the tensosensitivity of the borehole–aquifer system, which controls strain-to-hydrogeodynamic response [N1-F2]. In the Central Italy study, anomalies were detected in wells that were part of a monitoring test site in fractured carbonate aquifers, and the water-level responses were linked to specific mechanisms such as poroelastic response, undrained consolidation, clogging–unclogging, co-seismic gas bubble development, and shaking-induced compaction or dilatation [N2-F3]. This implies that anomalies are often site-specific and tied to local hydrogeology. The Yunnan radon study similarly notes that crustal activity and hydrogeological conditions are the main factors influencing anomalies [N1-F1].

Evidence for near-epicenter versus far-field anomalies is mixed. The hydrogeodynamic precursor review says that the largest anomalies tend to occur closest to the epicenter, while the same study notes that the correlation between precursor time and epicentral distance is not strong [N1-F2]. The Central Italy study also reports that “only a few studies have reported groundwater level variations induced by earthquakes that are very far away from the observation point, known as ‘teleseism’” [N2-F3]. It adds that seismic waves can cause oscillations in groundwater levels and that permanent offsets can occur after the event, but it does not establish a clear maximum distance in the provided evidence. The Yunnan study further notes a positive correlation between anomaly occurrence time and epicentral distance when epicentral distance is less than 300 km, which may be related to seismogenic modes and hydrogeological conditions [N1-F1]. Taken together, the evidence supports a general pattern: the closest anomalies are typically near the source, while detectable far-field anomalies are rare and require careful interpretation [N1-F2][N2-F3][N1-F1].

Earthquake magnitude appears to influence how far groundwater anomalies can be detected, but the relationship is not straightforward. The hydrogeodynamic precursor review states that precursor time and signal amplitude tend to increase with growing earthquake magnitude, while the relationship with epicentral distance is inverse [N1-F2]. The Central Italy study reports a clear correlation between earthquake distance and magnitude in hydrogeological responses [N2-F3]. This suggests that larger earthquakes can produce detectable anomalies farther away, at least under the right hydrogeological conditions. However, the review also cautions that the correlation is not sufficiently close, meaning magnitude alone does not fully explain the distance pattern [N1-F2].

Smaller earthquakes are harder to detect at distance because the hydrogeodynamic precursor literature suggests that the largest-amplitude anomalies tend to occur closest to the epicenter and that the precursor signal is strongly dependent on local hydrogeology [N1-R3][N1-F2]. In other words, small earthquakes may produce detectable anomalies, but only when the monitoring system is close enough and the site conditions are favorable. The Central Italy study also notes that “only a few studies have reported groundwater level variations induced by earthquakes that are very far away from the observation point” [N2-F3], implying that distant anomalies are rare and likely only visible in highly sensitive systems. The Yunnan radon study adds that the positive correlation between anomaly occurrence time and epicentral distance is only evident for distances less than 300 km, and that this may reflect seismogenic modes and hydrogeological conditions rather than a universal rule [N1-F1]. Thus, the evidence supports a general trend that larger earthquakes can produce detectable anomalies farther away, but smaller earthquakes are harder to detect at distance because their signals are weaker and more localized [N1-F2][N2-F3][N1-F1].

Magnitude alone does not fully explain the distance pattern. The hydrogeodynamic precursor review explicitly states that precursor time and signal amplitude do not show sufficiently close correlative relationships with earthquake magnitude and epicentral distance [N1-F2]. This means that other factors—such as aquifer properties, tectonic setting, and monitoring network density—are also important. The Central Italy study further emphasizes the need to distinguish between local and distant effects because probes used for earthquake precursor identification are also affected by distant earthquakes [N2-F3]. In that context, network density and monitoring coverage are crucial: the study says that identifying and filtering the effect of distant earthquakes is a prerequisite to understanding the possible effect induced by nearby faults [N2-F3]. So the conclusion is that magnitude matters, but it is not the only determinant; local hydrogeology, network density, and temporal resolution also shape how far anomalies can be detected [N1-F2][N2-F3][N1-F1].

The historical examples in the evidence show that groundwater anomalies can precede earthquakes, but the distance from the event and the monitoring setup affect whether those anomalies are visible. The strongest direct historical case in the evidence is the Turkish spring-water study, which documents hydrogeochemical anomalies in spring waters before two Mw 5.0 earthquakes: the December 4, 2023, Mudanya earthquake in the Marmara region and the January 27, 2024, Kuşadası earthquake in the Aegean Extensional Province [N3-F4]. In those cases, distinct electrical conductivity and ion anomalies lasting at least 30 days were observed at Sap-01 and Naz-01 sites before the earthquakes [N3-F4]. The study also notes that no significant anomalies were detected in samples from other springs, likely because they were off-fault or on different tectonic blocks [N3-F4]. This indicates that location is important: anomalies may be visible near active fault zones but not in nearby areas that are geologically separated [N3-F4].

The evidence also includes broader historical precedent. The hydrogeodynamic precursor review states that hydrogeodynamic precursors were registered before 31 earthquakes with magnitudes between 4.5 and 8.0 [N1-F2]. This suggests that groundwater anomalies have been documented for earthquakes ranging from moderate to large, but the review does not provide a single maximum distance for all events. The Yunnan radon study also documents precursory anomalies before earthquakes, though its main focus is on the radon signal and its relation to distance and hydrogeological conditions [N1-F1]. In addition, the review mentions the 1990s Kamchatka earthquakes in the context of hydrogeochemical anomalies in groundwater and gas before earthquakes [N3-R2], and the broader literature cited in the Turkish study includes many other historical and regional examples [N3-F4].

How far before the event the anomalies were detected is somewhat uneven in the evidence. The Turkish study notes that anomalies were observed at least 30 days before the earthquakes [N3-F4], which is a relatively long lead time. The hydrogeodynamic precursor review does not specify a fixed lead time but does emphasize that precursor time correlates with the event magnitude [N1-F2]. The Yunnan study reports that precursor anomalies were identified using 1000-day continuous data and that the anomaly occurrence time correlates with epicentral distance for distances under 300 km [N1-F1]. That suggests that anomalies may be detectable days to months in advance, depending on the system and monitoring frequency [N1-F1][N3-F4].

Event size and location strongly influence anomaly visibility. The Turkish study clearly shows that anomalies were absent in off-fault or tectonically separated springs, indicating that fault proximity and geological structure matter [N3-F4]. The hydrogeodynamic precursor review also states that the largest amplitude precursory anomalies tend to occur before the largest magnitude earthquakes [N3-R5], while the same review notes that the relationship between precursor time and epicentral distance is not sufficiently close [N1-F2]. In other words, larger earthquakes may produce more detectable anomalies, but local hydrogeology and tectonic setting are still decisive. The Central Italy study further shows that anomalies can be produced by distant earthquakes, but those effects are rare and require careful filtering from local signals [N2-F3].

The evidence also indicates that some anomalies are confirmed while others are possibly false positives. The Turkish study says that the findings highlight the importance of geological knowledge in selecting sampling sites, and it warns that no significant anomalies were detected in some springs because of their off-fault or different tectonic-block locations [N3-F4]. This is a strong indication that not all anomalies are true precursors; some may reflect sampling bias, local hydrogeological conditions, or unrelated factors. The review on false positives and the broader discussion of precursor ambiguity in the groundwater literature also support the idea that anomalies can be misleading unless carefully contextualized [N4-R5]. So the overall picture is that historical events show groundwater anomalies can precede earthquakes, but visibility depends on earthquake size, location, hydrogeology, and monitoring design, and not all anomalies are unequivocally confirmed [N1-F2][N3-F4][N3-R2][N2-F3].

Interpreting groundwater anomalies as earthquake precursors is limited by several caveats. First, false positives and non-seismic causes are common. The evidence shows that groundwater changes can result from meteorological factors, seasonal variation, and other hydrological causes [N1-F1][N2-F3]. The Turkish study explicitly notes that anomalous radon and other geochemical signals may be affected by sampling location and tectonic setting, and that some springs did not show anomalies because they were off-fault or on different tectonic blocks [N3-F4]. The review on false positives also states that “the curse of the false positive” is a major challenge for earthquake precursor research [N4-R5]. In addition, the review of hydrogeodynamic precursors notes that precursor time and signal amplitude do not show sufficiently close correlative relationships with magnitude and distance, so anomalies may not reliably indicate an imminent earthquake [N1-F2].

Sampling density and temporal resolution are important limitations. The Yunnan study uses 1000-day continuous data from 8 monitoring stations and identifies anomalies using autocorrelation and variance [N1-F1]. The Central Italy study uses continuous groundwater-level monitoring at 5-minute intervals and notes that transient and permanent signals can be symptomatic of different mechanisms [N2-F3]. The machine learning and borehole strain studies also emphasize the need for long-term, high-resolution monitoring networks [N4-R1][N4-R2]. This suggests that sparse or low-resolution sampling can miss subtle anomalies or misinterpret them as precursors. The Turkish study further emphasizes the need for long-term, high-resolution continuous monitoring networks to better understand pre-earthquake signals [N3-F4].

Uncertainty affects distance and magnitude conclusions. The hydrogeodynamic precursor review states that the relationship between precursor time and epicentral distance is not sufficiently close, and that precursor time and signal amplitude increase with growing magnitude while the relationship with distance is inverse [N1-F2]. The Central Italy study similarly reports a clear correlation between earthquake distance and magnitude in hydrogeological responses, but it also notes that distinguishing local from distant effects requires filtering [N2-F3]. This means that conclusions about how far anomalies can be detected are uncertain without careful analysis of site-specific conditions. The Yunnan study adds that the positive correlation between anomaly occurrence time and epicentral distance is only evident for distances less than 300 km, and that it may depend on seismogenic modes and hydrogeological conditions [N1-F1]. So the evidence supports a cautious conclusion: anomalies can indicate seismic stress, but their distance and magnitude interpretation is highly uncertain.

Anomalies may still be ambiguous even with monitoring because the underlying physical mechanisms are complex and overlapping. The Central Italy study describes groundwater responses as being linked to multiple mechanisms such as poroelastic response, undrained consolidation, clogging–unclogging, co-seismic gas bubble development, and shaking-induced compaction or dilatation [N2-F3]. This complexity means that the same signal can arise from different causes, including distant earthquakes, seasonal variation, or hydrological noise [N2-F3][N4-R5]. The Yunnan study also notes that radon anomalies are difficult to identify because concentrations often show nonlinear dynamic fluctuations [N1-F1]. Taken together, the evidence shows that groundwater anomalies can be useful, but their interpretation as earthquake precursors is limited by false positives, non-seismic causes, sparse sampling, low temporal resolution, and uncertain mechanistic interpretation [N1-F1][N2-F3][N3-F4][N4-R5].

## How far from an earthquake’s epicenter have precursory groundwater anomalies been detected?

The evidence suggests that precursory groundwater anomalies are most commonly detected **near the epicenter**, but some studies also report anomalies at **more distant locations**. The clearest pattern is that the **largest-amplitude anomalies tend to occur closest to the epicenter**, and the greatest anomalies are reported closest to the epicenters, especially for the largest earthquakes [N1-R3][N1-F2]. In hydrogeodynamic studies, precursory anomalies tend to occur close to the eventual epicenter of the earthquake, and physical models indicate this proximity is tied to hydrogeological and geodynamic conditions [N1-R2][N1-F2]. At the same time, the evidence also shows that detectable far-field anomalies are rare: “only a few studies have reported groundwater level variations induced by earthquakes that are very far away from the observation point” [N2-F3]. The Yunnan radon study further notes a **positive correlation between anomaly occurrence time and epicentral distance when epicentral distance is less than 300 km**, which may be related to seismogenic modes and hydrogeological conditions [N1-F1].

So the overall range of distances is **near-epicenter to occasionally far-field**, with the most reliable anomalies usually found within a few hundred kilometers, and only very rare reports of detectable anomalies hundreds of kilometers away [N1-F2][N2-F3][N1-F1].

## What types of groundwater signals have been observed?

The evidence points to a broad range of groundwater signals, not just one class of anomaly. The most direct groundwater precursor evidence comes from **groundwater radon anomalies**, identified using critical slowing down theory in a Yunnan case study [N1-F1]. The hydrogeodynamic precursor review explicitly documents **groundwater level variations** before earthquakes and notes that these precursors were registered by variations of groundwater level before 31 earthquakes with magnitudes between 4.5 and 8.0 [N1-F2]. Additional studies link groundwater responses to earthquakes to changes in **groundwater level, temperature, water chemistry, and gas geochemistry** [N2-F3]. A Turkish spring-water study documents **electrical conductivity and ion concentration changes** in spring waters before moderate-magnitude earthquakes [N3-F4].

In short, the anomalies observed include:
- groundwater level changes [N1-F2][N2-F3]
- radon anomalies [N1-F1]
- electrical conductivity and ion concentration anomalies [N3-F4]
- temperature and water chemistry changes [N2-F3]

These signals are not mutually exclusive, and the same study may use multiple types of groundwater monitoring to identify pre-earthquake changes.

## Are anomalies localized or regional?

The evidence strongly favors **localized anomalies** rather than widespread regional anomalies. Earthquake magnitude does appear to influence how far anomalies can be detected, but the relationship is **not straightforward**. - **Smaller earthquakes are harder to detect at distance** [N1-R3][N1-F2]
- **Magnitude alone is not enough; hydrogeology and monitoring conditions matter** [N1-F2][N2-F3][N1-F1]

The historical evidence shows that groundwater anomalies can precede earthquakes, but visibility depends on **earthquake size, location, hydrogeology, and monitoring design**. The evidence suggests that not all groundwater anomalies are unequivocally confirmed. Interpreting groundwater anomalies as earthquake precursors is limited by several caveats:

Groundwater changes can result from **meteorological factors**, **seasonal variation**, and **other hydrological causes**, not just earthquakes [N1-F1][N2-F3].
